hook_text: One loose lead turns a torch circuit into a heater. Here is how to connect circuits right, and how to draw them so anyone can read them.
clip_script: A circuit is a loop: out of plus, through every part, back to minus. Break it anywhere and everything stops, so trace it with your finger first, clips on metal, joints tight. Some parts have a right way round: the cell's button is plus; the LED's long leg is the anode; swap a motor's wires and it reverses. Now the danger: clip a lead across the bulb. The bulb goes out and the lead gets warm, because current takes the easy path and nothing is left to resist it. That is a short, the number one cause of electrical fires. Fuses melt, breakers trip, and the earth-leakage saves the person, not the wire. Then the language: cell is a long line and a short line, lamp a circle with a cross, resistor a box, switch a gap, LED a triangle with arrows, dots where wires join. Ruled rectangle, plus on the left, switch open. Read it by tracing the loop and hunting for shortcuts.
visual_style: Whiteboard loop with a finger tracing it; a lead snaps across a bulb, the bulb dims to black and the lead glows orange; a fuse wire melts; a symbol chart assembles into a neat ruled circuit diagram.
pacing: The loop, polarity, the short, protection, the symbols.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw the circuit of a torch using only standard symbols.
